analysis.one_liner: Lets student loans be wiped out in bankruptcy like other debts.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on September 30, 2022 and died there when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, student loans can only be erased in bankruptcy if the borrower proves the debt causes an 'undue hardship' — a standard so strict that most borrowers never even try. This bill would delete that exception, letting student loans be discharged in bankruptcy the same way credit card debt, medical debt, and business loans can be. It died without any committee vote or floor action.
analysis.who_benefits: Student borrowers whose loans have become unpayable — particularly older borrowers and people who attended for-profit colleges or dropped out without earning a credential — would gain the same bankruptcy escape hatch available to almost every other kind of debtor. Currently many borrowers pay on loans they will never finish repaying because bankruptcy offers no realistic way out.

how_it_helps.text: Deletes the bankruptcy-law exception (11 U.S.C. § 523(a)(8)) that currently bars discharging student loans unless the debtor proves an 'undue hardship,' making student loans dischargeable like most other unsecured debt.
Strikes the matching provision in Chapter 13 confirmation (§ 1328(a)(2)) so borrowers completing a court-approved repayment plan can also have remaining student loans wiped out.
Applies only to bankruptcy cases filed on or after the date of enactment, so it does not reopen closed cases.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government's student loan program would absorb larger losses when borrowers discharge federal loans in bankruptcy, a cost ultimately carried by taxpayers. Private student lenders and loan servicers would lose their current protection against bankruptcy discharge, and defenders of the current rule argue lenders would price that risk into all student loans, potentially raising rates or tightening credit for future borrowers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal loan program and student lenders

drawbacks.text: Wiping out student debt in bankruptcy would increase losses in the federal loan program, which are ultimately borne by taxpayers, since the government already absorbs most defaults without any discharge mechanism.

Critics of loosening the standard argue lenders and the loan program would raise rates or restrict credit to offset the new discharge risk, raising costs for all future borrowers — a cost the bill does not address.
The bill contains no procedural safeguards or waiting periods, so unlike some reform proposals it gives courts no middle path between the current near-total bar and fully routine discharge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers trapped in unpayable debt, the change is straightforward relief, and it treats student loans like every other kind of consumer debt, which is the honest baseline. The real tradeoff is financial: the federal loan program would take bigger bankruptcy losses, and credit terms for future students could tighten. A more detailed version could stage the relief or pair it with program financing, but this bill offered a clean, simple rule and no guardrails.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its bankruptcy subcommittee for the final three months of the Congress and was never brought up for a vote before the session ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the bill on September 30, 2022, with 11 Democratic cosponsors including several members of the Judiciary Committee, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
On November 1, 2022, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law, which handled bankruptcy matters.
No markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
Under current law retained by the bill's failure, student loans are dischargeable in bankruptcy only if the debtor proves the debt imposes an 'undue hardship,' a standard many borrowers cannot meet.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal student loan program and private student lenders are better off: the bankruptcy exception they rely on stays on the books, and struggling borrowers remain largely unable to discharge their loans. No one acted to block a vote; the bill simply ran out of time at the end of a session without ever reaching one.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Student loan program and private lenders

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to his own committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 initial sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsor joined; the bill never advanced far enough for a recorded vote, so no roll-call shows the full split.

industries.note: The bill removes the bankruptcy exception that currently guarantees these loans survive almost any bankruptcy, so lenders and servicers would lose their strongest collection protection. Its interest runs against borrowers who want the same discharge rights other debtors have.

The Department of Education would recover less from borrowers who discharge federal loans in bankruptcy, increasing program costs borne by taxpayers. Some of those losses would offset hardship the program currently forces borrowers to carry.
Allowing student loan discharge would expand the workload of bankruptcy practice and the courts that handle it, and borrowers who file would directly benefit from the same representation.
